title: Intersection Types & Function Overloads
description: Combine types with &, build mixin patterns, and write functions with multiple typed call signatures.

challenges.title: What is an intersection type?
challenges.whyMatters: Intersection types are how you compose behaviours — a logged service, a retryable client, an auditable config all combine multiple concerns into one type.
hints: & means the value must satisfy ALL constituent types simultaneously

choices.label: { name: string } — only the last type matters
{ createdAt: string } | { name: string } — either property is enough
{ createdAt: string; name: string } — must have ALL properties from both types
never — two types cannot be merged

challenges.title: Intersection vs union
challenges.whyMatters: Confusing & with | is one of the most common TypeScript mistakes. Knowing the difference immediately is fundamental.
hints: Union: only shared properties are safe. Intersection: all properties from both are available.

choices.label: Union: x and y  ·  Intersection: neither without narrowing
Union: neither x nor y without narrowing  ·  Intersection: both x and y
They are identical — & and | are aliases
Union: y only  ·  Intersection: x only

challenges.title: Function overload signatures
challenges.whyMatters: Overloads let callers get the precise return type based on what they pass in — no union in, no union out. Used in every well-typed utility library.
hints: The implementation signature is not visible to callers — only the overload signatures are

choices.label: parse('5') returns number  ·  parse(5) returns string  ·  implementation signature is private to the function body
The implementation signature is the one callers see
Overloads are only for classes, not standalone functions

challenges.title: Write intersection-based mixin types
challenges.description:
Define these composable types and functions:

  type Identifiable = { id: string }
  type Timestamped = { createdAt: string; updatedAt: string }
  type Auditable = { createdBy: string; updatedBy: string }

Derive:
  type Entity = Identifiable & Timestamped
  type AuditedEntity = Entity & Auditable

Write:
- `createEntity(id: string): Entity` — sets id, createdAt and updatedAt to current ISO string
- `withAudit(entity: Entity, user: string): AuditedEntity` — adds audit fields to an existing entity
- `isAudited(e: Entity | AuditedEntity): e is AuditedEntity` — type guard checking for audit fields
challenges.whyMatters: Mixin types built with & are how you model layered concerns — every database record, audit log, and event sourcing system uses this pattern.
hints: withAudit: spread entity and add createdBy/updatedBy
isAudited: check 'createdBy' in e && 'updatedBy' in e

challenges.title: Intersection with function types
challenges.description:
What type does `Callable` represent here, and what can you do with a value of this type?

  type Loggable = { log(msg: string): void }
  type Callable = (() => void) & Loggable

  declare const fn: Callable
  fn()         // ?
  fn.log('x')  // ?
challenges.whyMatters: Functions with attached properties appear in real APIs — Express middleware, event emitters, CLI command objects. Intersection types are how you type them.
hints: Callable is both a function and an object with a log method — both usages are valid

choices.label: fn() errors — you can only call it as fn.log()
fn() works (it's a function) and fn.log('x') works (it has the Loggable shape) — both are valid
Intersection of a function and object type is always never
fn.log('x') errors — function types cannot have properties

challenges.title: Write function overloads
challenges.description:
Write these overloaded functions:

1. `format(value: string): string` — pads to 10 chars with spaces on the right
   `format(value: number): string` — formats with 2 decimal places
   `format(value: boolean): string` — returns 'yes' or 'no'

2. `lookup(map: Record<string, string>, key: string): string`
   `lookup(map: Record<string, string>, key: string, fallback: string): string`
   — returns map[key] or throws if not found (no fallback), or returns fallback (with fallback)

3. `coerce(val: string): number`
   `coerce(val: number): string`
   — converts between string and number
challenges.whyMatters: Overloads are how well-typed utility libraries avoid returning messy union types at every call site. Every time you've used a library function that knows its return type from its argument, overloads made that possible.
hints: Write overload signatures first, then the implementation with union types
format implementation: switch on typeof value
lookup: check if key in map for the no-fallback overload

challenges.title: Build a typed middleware chain
challenges.description:
Build a typed middleware system using intersection types:

  type Context = { path: string; method: string; body: unknown }
  type AuthContext = Context & { userId: string; role: 'admin' | 'user' }
  type LoggedContext = Context & { requestId: string; startedAt: number }
  type FullContext = AuthContext & LoggedContext

  type Middleware<In, Out extends In> = (ctx: In) => Out

Write:
- `withAuth(ctx: Context): AuthContext` — adds userId 'user-123' and role 'user'
- `withLogging(ctx: Context): LoggedContext` — adds requestId (random 8-char hex) and startedAt (Date.now())
- `compose<A, B extends A, C extends B>(m1: Middleware<A, B>, m2: Middleware<B, C>): Middleware<A, C>` — chains two middlewares
- Use compose to create `fullMiddleware: Middleware<Context, FullContext>`
challenges.whyMatters: Typed middleware chains are the backbone of every HTTP framework. This pattern shows how intersection types naturally model context enrichment — each middleware adds to what's available downstream.
hints: Spread the incoming context and add the two auth fields — use any placeholder values since this is a mock middleware
Generate a short random hex string for requestId — convert a random number to hex and slice to 8 characters
compose returns a new middleware function that feeds the output of the first middleware directly into the second
Apply compose with the two middleware functions — the order determines which enriches the context first; TypeScript infers the combined output type from the composition
